abbad@<B>abbad,</B> abbod, abbud, abbot, es; <I>m:</I> abboda, an; <I>m.</I> I. <I>an abbot;</I> abbās, -- the title of the male superior of certain religious establishments, thence called abbeys. The word <I>abbot</I> appears to have been, at first, applied to any member of the clerical order, just as the French Père and English Father. In the earliest age of monastic institutions the monks were not even priests: they were merely religious persons, who retired from the world to live in common, and the abbot was one of their number, whom they elected to preside over the association. In regard to general ecclesiastical discipline, all these communities were at this early time subject to the bishop of the diocese, and even to the pastor of the parochial district within the bounds of which they were established. At length it began to be usual for the abbot to be in orders; and since the sixth century monks generally have been priests. In point of dignity an abbot is generally next to a bishop. A minute account of the different descriptions of abbots may be found in Du Cange's Glossary, and in Carpentier's supplement to that work :-- Se ārwurða abbad Albīnus <I>the reverend abbot Albinus,</I> Bd. pref. Riht is ðæt abbodas fæste on mynstrum wunian <I>it is right that abbots dwell closely in their minsters,</I> L. I. P. 13; Th. ii. 320, 30. Her Forþrēd abbud forþfērde <I>in this year abbot Forthred died,</I> Chr. 803; Erl. 60, 13. Se abbot Saxulf <I>the abbot Saxulf,</I> Chr. 675; Ing. 50, 15. Swā gebireþ abbodan <I>as becometh abbots,</I> L. Const. W. p. 150, 27; L. I. P. 13; Th. ii. 320, 35. II. <I>bishops were sometimes subject to an abbot, as they were to the abbots of Iona</I> :-- Nū, sceal beōn ǣfre on Iī abbod, and nā biscop; and ðan sculon beōn underþeōdde ealle Scotta biscopas, forðan ðe Columba [MS. Columban] was abbod, nā biscop <I>now, in Iī</I> [<I>Iona</I>] <I>, there must ever be an abbot, not a bishop; and to him must all bishops of the Scots be subject, because Columba was an abbot, not a bishop,</I> Chr. 565; Th. 32, 10-16, col. l. [<I>Laym.</I> abbed: <I>O. Frs.</I> abbete: <I>N. Ger.</I> abt: <I>O. H. Ger.</I> abbat: <I>Lat.</I> abbas; <I>gen.</I> abbātis <I>an abbot: Goth.</I> abba : <I>Syr.</I> HEBREW abba <I>father,</I> from <I>Heb.</I> HEBREW ab <I>father, pl.</I> HEBREW abot <I>fathers.</I>] DER. abbad-dōm, -hād, -isse, -rīce: abboda.@abbad

abeodan@<B>ā-beōdan.</B> <I>Add:</I> (1) to announce, declare a message :-- Hē word ābeād <I>he delivered the words of his message,</I> B. 390. Ðæt hē hyre ǣrende ābude ðām bisceope ðysum wordum, Hml. S. 2, 68. Ðæt ic wiþ ðē sceolde ǣrendsprǣce ābeōdan, Räi. 61, 16. Āboden bið <I>praedicabitur</I>, Lk. R. 12, 3: 24, 47. (l a) where the message is given by a clause:-- Hē ābeād þæt ǣgðer ðāra folca ōþrum āgeāfe ealle ðā men ðe hiē gehergead hæfden, Ors. 4, 6; S. 178, 12. (2) <I>to announce</I> what is coming:-- Heāhengel hǣlo ābeād Marian, ðæt heō Meotod sceolde cennan, Men. 50: An. 96. Ðæt ðū hellwarum hyht ne ābeōde, ah ðū him secgan miht sorga mǣste, Sat. 695. Se deāþ him tō cymeþ Godes dōm tō ābeōdenne, Bl. H. 59, 12. (2 a) <I>to announce</I> the coming of a person:-- Hæfde hē seleweard āseted, sundornytte beheōld, eoton weard ābeād (<I>the guard's special office was to give notice of Grendel's coming</I>), B. 668. (3) in formulae of greeting, <I>to bid</I> farewell, (hǣl ābeōdan) <I>to hail:</I>-- Hē hǣlo ābeād heorðgeneātum <I>he bade farewell to</I><I>his comrades</I>, B. 2418. Hēht hē Elenan hǣl ābeōdan <I>he sent salutation to Elene</I>, El. 1004. (4) <I>to announce</I> what may be accepted, <I>to offer</I> :-- Nū ic dē cyst ābeād <I>lo! I have offered you a choice</I>, Gen. 1919. Fela gē mē earda āboden habbaþ, Gū. 280. (5) <I>to announce</I> what is to be obeyed, <I>to bid, command</I> :-- Hē up lōcade, swā se ār ābeād, El. 87 : Gen. 1362. Ābeād cyning þegnum sīnum, ðæt hiē . . . , 1869. Ðē ābeōdan hēt hē, ðæt ðū . . . , Gū. 1348. Engel stefne ābeād, hēt ðæt treōw ceorfan, Dan. 510. (6) <I>to summon, call</I> out :-- Hē fyrde hēt ūt ābeōdan, Chr. 1091 ; Erl. 227, 33. Ābeōdende <I>eliciens (igniferas fulminum coruscationes</I>, Ald. 62), Wrt. Voc. ii. 85, 46. Bið geban micel and āboden þider eal Adames cnōsl <I>omnes homines cogentur adesse</I>, Dōm. L. 128. [He his ærnde abed (bed, 2nd MS.), Lay. 4423. <I>O. H. Ger.</I> ar-biotan <I>exhibere, offerre: Ger.</I> er-bieten.]@a-beodan

aberan@<B>a-beran;</B> <I>p.</I> -bær; <I>pp.</I> -boren. I. <I>to bear, carry, suffer;</I> portare, ferre :-- Ðe man aberan ne mæg <I>which they are not able to bear,</I> Mt. Bos. 23, 4. Hī ne māgon nān earfoða aberan <I>they cannot bear any troubles,</I> Bt. 39, 10; Fox 228, 3: Andr. Kmbl. 1912; An. 958: Ps. Th. 54, 11. II. <I>to take</I> or <I>carry away;</I> tollere, auferre :-- Abær hine of eowdum sceāpa <I>sustulit eam de gregibus ovium,</I> Ps. Spl. 77, 76: Ps. Grn. 50,12. v. beran.@a-beran
aberan@<B>ā-beran</B>. <I>Add:</I> <B>I</B>. with sense of movement, (1) <I>to bear off, bring, carry</I> :-- Se hwæl hine ābær tō Niniuēa birig, Ælfc. T. Grn. 10, 13. Mid ðȳ wē ūre scyp fram ðām ȳþum upp ābǣron (<I>exportaremus</I>), Bd. 5, 1; S. 614, 11. Ic gaderode mē . . . ðā wlitegostan treōwo be ðām dǣle ðe ic āberan mihte; ne com ic mid ānre byrðene hām, ðe mē ne lyste ealne ðane wude hām brengan, gif ic hyne ealne āberan mihte. Shrn. 163, 5-11. (1 a) <I>reflex.</I> :-- Hē ongann tō ðām swȳðe cwacian and mid fōtum tealtian, ðæt hē uneāðe hine sylfne āberan mihte <I>coepit tremere, seque ipsum nutanti gressu vix posse portare</I>. Gr. D. 36, 21. (2) <I>to bring forth</I>, (a) <I>to bear</I> a child :-- Ðæt bearn ðe ābær ūrne Hǣlend, Hml. A. 25, 16 : Hml. Th. i. 198, 1. (b) <I>to bring</I> to light :-- Se goldhord ne mæg beōn forholen, nū hit swā upp is āboren, Hml. S. 23, 604. <B>II</B>. with sense of rest (metaph.). (1) <I>to bear with, tolerate</I> :-- Seō cyrice . . . swā ābireþ (<I>portat</I>) and ældeth, ðæt oft ðæt yfel āberende (<I>portando</I>) and yldende beweraþ, Bd. 1, 27; 8. 491, 31. (2) <I>to bear, endure, not to give way under</I> trial, suffering, &amp;c. :-- Hē þā wītu ābær <I>tormenta ferebat</I>, Bd. 1, 7; S. 477, 46. Hwæðer siō gecynd ðæs līchoman siē strang, and eāþelīce mæge ðā strangan lǣcedōmas āberan, Lch. ii. 84, 13. Se drenc wæs deādbǣre, ðā ðā hē ne mihte līfes tācn āberan (<I>the vessel containing the liquor had burst when the sign of the cross was made</I>), Hml. Th. ii. 158, 23. (3) <I>to bear, be under an obligation for</I> an imposition, &amp;c. :-- Ābere se borh ðæt hē āberan scolde, L. Edg. ii. 6; Th. i. 268, 9. [<I>Goth.</I> us-bairan <I>auferre, proferre, portare: O. H. Ger.</I> ar-beran <I>edere, afferre</I>.]@a-beran
